    title: High-risk path for systems that evaluate or place learners
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [B]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ai_assessment, ai_adaptive]
    requirement: >
      AI that evaluates learning outcomes, steers learning, assigns levels or monitors tests is
      treated as an Annex III high-risk candidate: risk management file, data governance, logging,
      human oversight, accuracy and robustness testing.
    rationale: AI Act Annex III(3). Obligations apply from 2 Dec 2027 under the Digital Omnibus.
    improvement: Open a risk management file now (templates/ai-risk-file.md) and record the classification decision.
    effort: high
    sources: [AIA, AIA-OMNIBUS]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: high_risk_without_risk_file, confidence: high}

  - id: B-EVL-02
    title: No camera-based or biometric proctoring of minors
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [B]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [assessment, ai_assessment]
    requirement: Tests are not proctored by webcam, eye tracking, keystroke biometrics or behaviour analysis of the child.
    rationale: AI Act Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition) and Annex III(3)(d) (monitoring during tests). GDPR Art. 9.
    improvement: Use supervised test conditions in class instead of automated surveillance.
    effort: medium
    sources: [AIA, GDPR]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(proctor|eyeTracking|gazeTracking|tabSwitchDetect|keystrokeDynamics|webcamMonitor)'}

  - id: B-EVL-03
    title: Results are explainable and contestable
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [B]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [assessment, ai_assessment]
    requirement: Teachers and learners can see why a result was given and can contest it with a human.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 22(3). AI Act transparency for high-risk systems.
    improvement: Show per-item evidence behind each score and a 'request review' action for teachers.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, AIA]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: B-EVL-04
    title: Validity, fairness and accessibility of assessment
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [B]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [assessment, ai_assessment]
    requirement: >
      Assessment validity is documented, results are checked for bias across groups (gender,
      language background, SEN), and accommodations (extra time, audio) do not disadvantage learners.
    rationale: Good assessment practice and AI Act data governance expectations.
    improvement: Run a differential item functioning check on pilot data and document accommodations.
    effort: high
    sources: [AIA, UNCRC-GC25]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: B-UGC-01
    title: User-generated content is moderated and visible to the teacher
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [B, A, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ugc, chat]
    requirement: >
      Content created or uploaded by children is moderated proportionally to age, visible to the
      responsible teacher, reportable, and not public. Uploaded media has metadata (e.g. GPS) stripped.
    rationale: DSA Art. 28 guidelines. KIDS Act Art. 12(3) and 19.
    improvement: Add teacher review queues, EXIF stripping on upload, and keep galleries class-private.
    effort: medium
    sources: [DSA-G28, KIDS, GDPR]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '(isPublic|visibility)\s*[:=]\s*[''"]?public'}

  - id: B-UGC-02
    title: No photos of children's faces kept or shared beyond need
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [B, A, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ugc]
    requirement: >
      Photos and videos of children are only stored when necessary for the learning activity, are
      never public, expire automatically, and others cannot download them.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 12(3)(e). GDPR minimisation and storage limitation.
    improvement: Prefer avatars; add auto-expiry and disable download of child media.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, GDPR]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: B-DAT-01
    title: Research use of learning data is separated
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [B, A, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Learning data is only shared for research under a data sharing agreement, with legal basis,
      ethics approval and pseudonymisation, and never as a by-product of normal operation. Research data
      come from a study build (CORE-DAT-25). Extracts use relative time (seconds since session start), drop
      the time zone, and never include the key between player codes and accounts: the controller keeps it.
    rationale: >
      GDPR Art. 5(1)(b), 6 and 89. A recipient without the key and without means reasonably likely to
      re-identify holds data that may not be personal for it, while they stay personal for the controller
      (CJEU, EDPS v SRB). CSEF still treats extracts about children as personal data.
    improvement: Create a research export pipeline that pseudonymises, uses relative time, keeps the key at home and logs every extract.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, CJEU-SRB, EDPB-PSEUDO]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: B-SIM-01
    title: Sensitive simulations include warnings and debrief
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [B]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: Simulations about health, conflict, loss or other sensitive themes include a content note, an exit at any time, and a guided debrief.
    rationale: Protects children from distressing content and supports reflection.
    improvement: Add content notes and a debrief screen designed with the instructional team.
    effort: low
    sources: [UNCRC-GC25, DSA-G28]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: B-OPS-01
    title: Dashboards show learning, not surveillance
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [A, B, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: Teacher and guardian dashboards show what helps learning; they avoid minute-by-minute activity logs and are explained to the child. Answers to personal questions follow CORE-DAT-17.
    rationale: Respect for the child's privacy and agency (KIDS Act Art. 20(1)(f), UN GC 25).
    improvement: Aggregate activity data and show learning progress instead of raw logs.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, UNCRC-GC25]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ================================================================ PROFILE C: gamified applications
  - id: C-ENG-01
    title: Streaks are optional and never punish
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [C, A]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [streaks]
    requirement: >
      Streaks can be switched off, carry no loss framing, and missing a day costs nothing (free
      freezes or no reset).
    rationale: "KIDS Act Art. 9(2)(d) (penalties for not engaging). DFA proposal: right to switch off streak rewards."
    improvement: Add a 'turn off streaks' setting and replace 'you will lose your streak' with neutral progress messages.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, DFA]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: high, flags: i, pattern: '(lose your streak|streak (will be )?lost|don''t break (your|the) (streak|chain)|perdes a tua sequ[eê]ncia|vais perder a sequ[eê]ncia|n[aã]o quebres a sequ[eê]ncia)'}
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '(resetStreak|streakReset|breakStreak)'}

  - id: C-ENG-02
    title: Leaderboards are class-scoped and pseudonymous
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [C, A]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [leaderboards]
    requirement: >
      Leaderboards are limited to the class or group, show avatars or nicknames, can be disabled
      by the teacher, and never publicly rank named children.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 11(3) (social comparison). GDPR minimisation.
    improvement: Scope leaderboards to class, use nicknames, add a teacher toggle, and consider showing personal bests only.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, GDPR, DSA-G28, R-HANUS2015, R-SAILER2020]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(globalLeaderboard|publicLeaderboard|worldRanking|leaderboard[^\n]{0,80}(fullName|full_name|realName))'}

  - id: C-ENG-03
    title: Points and badges have no money value
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: Points, badges and levels cannot be bought, sold or exchanged for money or goods.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 13. Keeps gamification about learning.
    improvement: Remove any purchase or exchange path for points.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, DFA]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(buyPoints|purchasePoints|buyXp|purchaseXp|redeemForCash|pointsToCredit)'}

  - id: C-ENG-04
    title: No variable reward schedules designed for engagement
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [C, A]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: Rewards are predictable and earned. Random bonus drops and slot-machine style surprises are avoided.
    rationale: Variable ratio rewards drive compulsive use. KIDS Act Art. 13(2) bans them in spending contexts on social and video services.
    improvement: Replace random bonuses with predictable milestones the child can see in advance.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, KIDS-COM, R-DECI1999, R-DIXON2013]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(randomBonus|surpriseReward|dailySpin|spinTheWheel|luckyDraw|roda_?da_?sorte)'}

  - id: C-ENG-05
    title: Engagement metrics balanced by wellbeing metrics
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [C, A]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: Product KPIs for minors include learning and wellbeing outcomes, not only time spent, sessions or retention.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 10(2) asks recommender optimisation to include quality and mental health metrics; good practice for every product.
    improvement: Add learning-gain and healthy-session-length metrics to the product dashboard and goals.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, KIDS-COM, EUKO, R-CERASOLI2014]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: C-ENG-06
    title: Challenges without anxiety timers for younger children
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [C, A]
    age_bands: [B1, B2, B3]
    requirement: Quests and challenges for under-13s avoid countdown timers and expiring rewards.
    rationale: Time pressure creates anxiety and drives compulsive return.
    improvement: Remove expiry from quests or extend them to the whole school term.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS-COM, UNCRC-GC25]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(expiresIn|countdown|timeLeft|questExpiry|tempo_?restante)'}

  # ================================================================ AGE-BAND MODIFIERS
  - id: AGE-B1-01
    title: Ages 3 to 5 use the product only with an adult in control
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B1]
    requirement: >
      No child account with credentials, no text input, no external links, no notifications to
      the child, audio-first instructions, and any AI conversation only with an adult present.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(d) and 15(1)(d): access below 13 only through tools for guardians.
      Art. 7(4)(b) sets 3 years as the floor for guardian-controlled access to video services.
    improvement: Route access through the guardian or teacher device; remove text inputs and outbound links.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, UNCRC-GC25]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, globs: ['*.html', '*.jsx', '*.tsx', '*.vue', '*.svelte'], pattern: '<a\s[^>]*href=[''"]https?://'}

  - id: AGE-B2-01
    title: Under 10, communication uses preset messages only
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B1, B2]
    features: [chat, multiplayer]
    requirement: No free-text chat. Communication uses preset phrases or emojis. External links are behind an adult gate.
    rationale: DSA Art. 28 guidelines on contact risks; KIDS Act Art. 12 and 15(1)(c).
    improvement: Replace chat input with a preset phrase picker.
    effort: medium
    sources: [DSA-G28, KIDS]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '(sendChatMessage|chatInput|ChatInput|freeTextChat)'}

  - id: AGE-B3-01
    title: Under 13, access is enabled and controlled by a guardian or the school
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B1, B2, B3]
    requirement: >
      Below 13, access to online games and AI conversational features is enabled and controlled
      through tools for guardians (or the school in educational deployments).
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(d) and 15(1)(d).
    improvement: Require a guardian or school account to activate the child's access and settings.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: AGE-B4-01
    title: Ages 13 to 15 respect the national consent age and limited features
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B4]
    requirement: >
      Where consent is the legal basis, guardian consent is obtained below the national age of
      digital consent (13 to 16 depending on Member State). Social features follow limited-account rules.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 8. KIDS Act Art. 6(2) for social and video features (13 to 14 only with guardian-set limited accounts).
    improvement: Read the national pack for the consent age and add a guardian consent step below it.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, KIDS, EDPB-CONSENT]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: AGE-B5-01
    title: Ages 16 to 17 keep protective defaults
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B5]
    requirement: >
      Older teenagers may change defaults themselves after clear information and explicit choice,
      but defaults stay protective and profiling-based recommendations stay off by default.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 11(2) (changes only above 15 with explicit consent) and 10(2)(b).
    improvement: Allow opt-in changes with a plain explanation; keep defaults protective.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ================================================================ CORE: design for learning (look, sound, motion)
  # From research gathered for the EDEH Quality Compass (Nov 2026). See framework/03-design-and-motivation.md.
  - id: CORE-ACC-04
    title: Moving content and sound can be paused
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Content that moves, scrolls or animates automatically for more than 5 seconds can be paused,
      stopped or hidden, and audio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds can be paused
      or muted.
    rationale: WCAG 2.2.2 and 1.4.2 (Level A), within the AA target of the European Accessibility Act. Uncontrolled motion distracts all learners and harms some.
    improvement: Add pause and mute controls to every auto-playing animation, video and background audio.
    effort: low
    sources: [WCAG22, EAA, EN301549]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-ACC-05
    title: Colour is never the only cue
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Right and wrong answers, states and instructions are signalled by shape, text, icon or sound as
      well as colour.
    rationale: WCAG 1.4.1 (Level A). About 1 in 12 boys has a colour vision deficiency, so colour-only feedback fails several children in every class.
    improvement: Add icons or text (tick, cross, label) next to colour feedback; test screens in greyscale.
    effort: low
    sources: [WCAG22, EAA]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-01
    title: Motion and sound can be turned down or off
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product honours the device's reduced-motion setting and offers in-app controls to reduce
      animation and sound, including motion triggered by the learner's own actions.
    rationale: >
      WCAG 2.3.3 (Level AAA) protects learners with vestibular disorders. Distracting motion and sound
      compete with the learning content for attention.
    improvement: Wrap animations in a reduced-motion check (CSS prefers-reduced-motion, useReducedMotion, platform accessibility APIs) and add 'calm mode' and sound sliders.
    effort: low
    sources: [W3C-233, WCAG22, R-SUNDARARAJAN2020]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: reduced_motion_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-DES-02
    title: Motion shows the content, not decoration
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Animation is used to show what is learned (a process, a change over time, a procedure).
      Decorative, celebratory or purely entertaining motion and interesting-but-irrelevant extras
      ("seductive details") are kept to a minimum.
    rationale: >
      Seductive details lower learning (g = -0.33, 58 studies). Animation that depicts the content
      improves it (g = 0.23, 140 comparisons). In e-books, story-carrying animation helps young
      children while hotspots and side games distract.
    improvement: For each animation, write down what it teaches. Remove or shorten the ones that teach nothing; move side games out of the learning path.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-SUNDARARAJAN2020, R-BERNEY2016, R-TAKACS2015]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-03
    title: Calm screens, especially under 8
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B1, B2]
    requirement: >
      Few elements compete on screen at once (as a guide, no more than four interactive or animated
      elements on the main screen for under-8s), and help is available as audio or pictures, not text only.
    rationale: >
      Busy visual environments increase off-task time in young children and affect autistic children
      most. A content analysis of 200 apps for under-8s found 95% showed more than four elements on
      the opening screen.
    improvement: Audit each screen's element count; move secondary elements into menus; add spoken help.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-FISHER2014, R-HANLEY2017, R-CAC2018, R-HIRSHPASEK2015]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-04
    title: Fantasy does not blur facts for young children
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [B1, B2]
    requirement: >
      When teaching facts about the real world to young children, use realistic images and plain
      language. Talking animals, impossible events and fantasy framing are kept for stories and play,
      not for factual content.
    rationale: >
      Human-like animals with human-like language reduced fact learning in 3 to 5-year-olds.
      Fantastical events, more than pace, reduced executive function in 4-year-olds.
    improvement: Review factual units for young children; replace anthropomorphic narration with realistic visuals or clearly separate story from fact.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-GANEA2014, R-LILLARD2011]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-05
    title: Visual style matches the concept, especially in maths
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Abstract concepts use simple, schematic visuals. Graphs and diagrams carry no decorative
      pictures. Concrete images are used to start, then faded towards abstract representations.
      Pleasant colours and friendly faces are welcome where they do not compete with the content.
    rationale: >
      Pictures inside graphs led 6 to 8-year-olds to count the pictures; generic symbols transfer
      better than concrete ones. Schematic visuals outperform cartoon and realistic ones in learning
      games. Emotional design (pleasant colours, faces) improves retention (d = 0.39).
    improvement: Remove decoration from graphs and diagrams; plan concrete-to-abstract fading in maths sequences; keep warm, pleasant colour palettes.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-KAMINSKI2013, R-WOUTERS2013, R-BROM2018]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-06
    title: Celebrations are short and proportional
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Reward animations and sounds are brief, proportional to the achievement and skippable. Win
      sounds are not used to make small or no progress feel like a big win.
    rationale: >
      Each celebration is itself a seductive detail competing for attention. In slot machines, win
      sounds made players overestimate how often they won.
    improvement: Cap celebration length (e.g. under 2 seconds), scale them to the achievement, and allow skipping.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-SUNDARARAJAN2020, R-DIXON2013]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: dependency, confidence: medium, names: [canvas-confetti, react-confetti, react-canvas-confetti, js-confetti, party-js, confetti-js]}

  - id: CORE-DES-07
    title: No colour-psychology claims
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Design decisions and product claims do not rely on popular colour-psychology effects
      (e.g. "red lowers performance") that are not supported by robust evidence.
    rationale: The red-colour effect on cognitive performance does not survive correction for publication bias.
    improvement: Justify colour choices by function (contrast, coding, highlighting) and accessibility, not by colour-psychology claims.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-GNAMBS2020]
    detection:
      method: manual


  - id: CORE-DES-08
    title: Families and lives are shown without one default model
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Content about families, homes and daily life does not assume one model (a mother and a father,
      living grandparents, siblings, a room of one's own, holidays, money for extras). Every activity
      works with any answer, including "I don't have one" and "I'd rather not say", and families of
      many shapes appear in examples and illustrations. Themes such as loss, illness, separation or
      moving home come with a content note for the teacher, a calm exit for the child and a debrief.
    rationale: >
      Children in care, bereaved, in single-parent, same-sex-parent or reconstituted families, or
      living in poverty should not feel excluded or have to explain themselves (non-discrimination,
      UN General Comment 25). Same aim as B-SIM-01, for every profile and every content type.
      Inclusion is one of the EU quality criteria for digital education content.
    improvement: Review family-themed content with a teacher and a school psychologist, add "I don't have one" paths, and add content notes for sensitive themes.
    effort: low
    sources: [UNCRC-GC25, EU-DEC, ET4G2]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ================================================================ MOTIVATION (profiles A, B, C)
  - id: A-MOT-01
    title: Rewards are for learning, and the inventory shows it
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [A, B, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Points, stars and unlocks are tied to learning progress or effort, not to time spent, number of
      sessions or returning at set times. The team keeps a reward inventory (points, coins, badges, streaks,
      levels, leaderboards, unlockables, celebrations) and records for each one whether it is given for
      learning or for showing up. No more than two layers are given for playing time, logging in or simply
      finishing.
    rationale: >
      Expected rewards for doing a task lower later intrinsic motivation (d = -0.36), more in children.
      Badges plus leaderboards lowered motivation and exam scores over a semester. Each extra layer makes
      rewards more expected and more controlling. Aligning game mechanics with learning mechanics (LM-GM)
      avoids engagement for its own sake. Merges A-ECO-04 (retired in 0.11.0). Related: C-ENG-01 (streaks),
      C-ENG-04 (variable rewards), A-MOT-03 (rewards off), CORE-DES-06 (celebrations).
    improvement: Write the reward inventory (one line per layer, 'for learning' or 'for showing up'); map each reward to a learning mechanic (LM-GM); remove or convert layers given for time, logins or showing up.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-DECI1999, R-HANUS2015, R-MEKLER2017, R-SAILER2020, R-RADESKY2022, ARNAB2014, KIDS-COM, R-HIRSHPASEK2015]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: reward_layers, confidence: medium}


  - id: A-MOT-02
    title: Feedback informs, it does not control
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [A, B, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Feedback says what the learner did well and why, and what to try next. Copy avoids controlling
      language ("you must", "you have to") and external goal framing ("do this to win coins").
    rationale: >
      Informational verbal feedback raised intrinsic motivation (+0.33). Controlling language and
      external goal framing undermined conceptual learning in 11 to 12-year-olds, while drill scores
      looked fine, so the loss is easy to miss.
    improvement: Rewrite feedback strings as specific, informational messages; review copy for 'must' and reward-centred goals.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-DECI1999, R-VANSTEENKISTE2005]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(you must (finish|complete|play|keep)|you have to (finish|play|keep)|play to earn|win (more )?coins|tens de (acabar|jogar|continuar)|joga para ganhar)'}

  - id: A-MOT-03
    title: The product works with rewards switched off
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [A, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      The teacher can switch off points, leaderboards and celebrations, or turn competition into a
      shared class or team goal, and the activity still makes sense. Teacher materials include debrief
      prompts that turn rewards into information ("What did you do to earn that?").
    rationale: >
      Gamification's cognitive gains are robust, but motivational gains vanish in rigorous studies;
      competition combined with collaboration beats competition alone. Leaderboards reward those
      already ahead and hurt the weakest.
    improvement: Add teacher toggles for each reward layer and a 'team goal' mode; add debrief questions to the teacher guide.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-SAILER2020, R-HANUS2015, R-HIRSHPASEK2015]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: A-MOT-04
    title: Room for curiosity
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [A, B, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      The design includes open questions, things to explore, choices with consequences, and moments
      where learners explain their reasoning to each other. Success is not only a count of completed items.
    rationale: >
      Curiosity improves memory through the same reward circuit that responds to coins, and predicts
      achievement, more strongly for children in poverty. Intrinsic motivation predicts quality of work
      and well-being; incentives predict quantity. Intrinsic motivation already declines through school.
    improvement: Add at least one exploratory or explain-your-reasoning moment per unit; track learning quality, not only items completed.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-GRUBER2014, R-SHAH2018, R-CERASOLI2014, R-HOWARD2021, R-LEPPER2005]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: A-MOT-05
    title: Helping and creativity are recognised, not paid
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [A, B, C]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Helping others and cooperating are not paid with points or items. Creative tasks reward creative
      quality with informative feedback, not mere completion.
    rationale: >
      Toddlers rewarded with a toy for helping later helped less. Rewards for completing creative tasks
      lower creativity; recognising creative quality with fair feedback can help.
    improvement: Replace point payouts for helping with acknowledgement; give creative tasks qualitative feedback instead of completion rewards.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-WARNEKEN2008, R-BYRON2012]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ================================================================ COMMERCIAL PRACTICES (KIDS Act Recital 31, Art. 13)
  - id: CORE-COM-05
    title: Purchases are labelled as purchases, in real time
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [purchases]
    requirement: >
      Before any purchase or spending of purchasable currency, the child is told in clear, age-appropriate
      words (and icons or audio for non-readers) that this is a purchase that costs real money, at the
      moment it happens, with the price in the national currency.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 13(1) and Recital 31: minors often do not understand the consequences of online
      transactions, so purchases must be labelled as economic transactions in real time. Binding for social
      and video services and AI chatbots (Art. 14(1)(c)); applied to games and learning apps as good practice.
    improvement: Add a purchase confirmation screen for child accounts that says "This costs money" with the euro price and requires an adult step.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, UCPD, CPC-VC, DFA]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-COM-06
    title: No design for impulsive or unwanted spending
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [purchases]
    requirement: >
      No one-tap or in-content purchases for children. There is a clear separation and friction between
      learning or play content and buying anything related to it (for example a separate adult area and a
      confirmation step). No spending prompts at moments of frustration, failure or excitement.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 13(2) and Recital 31: services must not be designed in a way that leads to excessive,
      impulsive or unwanted spending, including through separation or friction between content and
      purchases. CPC Key Principle 7 asks for purchase prompts clearly separate from gameplay, and holds
      business models that depend on a few heavy spenders to a stricter fairness standard. DFA proposal
      targets the same practices.
    improvement: Move every purchase out of the child experience into a guardian or school area; remove purchase buttons from gameplay, results and failure screens.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, DFA, UCPD, CPC-VC, R-RADESKY2022]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '(oneClick(Buy|Purchase)|oneTap(Buy|Purchase)|instantPurchase|quickBuy|skipPurchaseConfirm(ation)?|autoPurchase|purchaseWithoutConfirm)'}

  - id: CORE-COM-07
    title: No disguised advertising
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Paid promotion is never presented as learning content, game content or a character's own opinion.
      Any sponsorship, product placement or brand partnership is clearly identified as such, in words a
      child of the target age understands.
    rationale: >
      UCPD Annex I point 11 bans editorial content paid for by a trader without making that clear, and
      point 28 bans direct exhortations to children to buy. DSA Art. 26 requires ads on platforms to be
      clearly identifiable. KIDS Act Recital 31 names product placement, influencer marketing and
      sponsorship as tactics with particular persuasive effects on minors.
    improvement: Label any commercial content clearly (e.g. "Ad" or "Paid partnership" with an icon); remove promotion voiced by characters or tutors.
    effort: low
    sources: [UCPD, DSA, KIDS]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(sponsoredBy|isSponsored|productPlacement|brandedContent|paidPartnership|partnerContent|conte[uú]do patrocinado|patrocinado por)'}

  - id: CORE-COM-08
    title: No commercial content inside learning activities for children
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Learning activities for children contain no product placement, branded rewards, sponsored
      characters or influencer endorsements, even when labelled. Funding and partner credits, if any,
      appear only in adult-facing areas.
    rationale: >
      Children, especially under 8, struggle to recognise persuasive intent even when content is labelled.
      Recital 31 of the KIDS Act lists these tactics among those with particular persuasive effects on
      minors; UN General Comment 25 asks states to protect children from commercial exploitation.
    improvement: Remove brands and sponsored items from learning content; move partner credits to the teacher or guardian area.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, UNCRC-GC25, R-RADESKY2022]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-COM-09
    title: Clear purchase information and a working right of withdrawal
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [purchases]
    requirement: >
      Before any purchase, with money or with purchasable currency, the buyer sees in plain words what is
      being bought, who sells it and how to contact them, the real-world price, whether and how the right of
      withdrawal applies, the legal guarantee, and how payment and delivery work. The buyer can withdraw
      within 14 days, and unused purchased currency can be returned in that time. For digital content the
      right is lost only after a separate, express consent to immediate delivery and an acknowledgement of
      losing it, confirmed afterwards. Paying with personal data does not remove it.
    rationale: >
      Consumer Rights Directive Art. 6 (pre-contractual information) and Art. 9 to 16 (withdrawal), as the
      EU consumer authorities read them for games in CPC Key Principles 4 and 5. Missing purchase information
      and withdrawal rights are among the issues in the CPC Network's coordinated actions on games.
    improvement: Add an information screen before every purchase; add a 14-day withdrawal path, unused currency included; make the digital-content waiver a separate, explicit step and confirm it on the receipt.
    effort: medium
    sources: [CRD, CPC-VC, CPC-JS, UCPD]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(all sales (are )?final|non-?refundable|no refunds?\b|not eligible for (a )?refund|n[ãa]o (é )?reembols[áa]vel|sem (direito a )?reembolso)'}


  - id: CORE-COM-10
    title: Fair, plain terms for purchases and accounts
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [purchases]
    requirement: >
      Terms for the game, purchases and currency are in plain language and do not limit statutory rights.
      They do not let the trader remove or change bought content or currency, or change the currency's
      value, on its own; content that players can reasonably expect to keep stays available. An account ban,
      suspension or removal comes with a reason and a way to contest it.
    rationale: >
      Unfair Contract Terms Directive Art. 3 and 5, as read by CPC Key Principle 6. For online platforms, DSA
      Art. 17 and 20 also require reasons and an internal complaint system for suspensions. Terms are written
      for adults; the child-friendly summary is in CORE-DAT-12.
    improvement: Rewrite currency and account terms in plain language; remove clauses that allow one-sided changes or removal; add a reasoned notice and an appeal for bans and suspensions.
    effort: medium
    sources: [UCTD, CPC-VC, DSA]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(reserves? the right to|may at any time)[^.\n]{0,40}(change|modify|remove|revoke|delete|adjust)[^.\n]{0,60}(virtual currency|currency|coins|gems|items|purchases)'}


  # ================================================================ AI COMPANIONS AND CHATBOTS (KIDS Act Recitals 32-34, Art. 14)
  - id: CORE-AI-08
    title: Conversation memory is off by default
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      AI systems do not keep or reuse information from a child's previous conversations by default,
      except where necessary to protect the child's safety. Any memory is visible to the teacher or
      guardian and can be deleted.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(b) and Recital 32: persistent conversational memory with minors must be disabled
      by default, to prevent accumulating sensitive data and reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.
      GDPR data minimisation and storage limitation.
    improvement: Start each session without past context; if continuity is needed for learning progress, store structured progress data (e.g. skills mastered), not chat transcripts.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, GDPR]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '(persistentMemory|longTermMemory|conversationMemory|memoryEnabled|rememberConversations|enableMemory)\s*[:=]\s*true'}

  - id: CORE-AI-09
    title: AI is red-teamed before release, re-tested regularly and monitored
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      Before release, AI features are red-teamed with a prompt set per age band and language. They are
      re-tested at regular intervals and on every model or prompt change. After release, incidents involving
      children are detected, logged, assessed and acted on, with a named owner.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 14(1)(e)(f) and Recitals 32 and 33. The legal duty of post-market monitoring does not
      apply to micro and small enterprises; CSEF applies it to every provider because the risk to a child
      does not depend on company size. Risk mitigations by the provider of the underlying general-purpose
      model (AI Act Art. 55) can be relied on in part, but are not sufficient on their own.
    improvement: Build a red-team prompt set per age band and language; run it in CI on prompt changes and at least each term; add an incident channel for teachers and guardians and a monthly review.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, AIA]
    detection:
      method: manual


  - id: CORE-AI-10
    title: An AI assistant inside a game or app is opt-in and easy to leave
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      When an AI chatbot or companion is a feature of a game, app or platform, it is not switched on
      automatically, not displayed prominently (e.g. not pinned at the top of contacts or the home screen),
      children are not encouraged to use it, and they can turn it off easily at any time.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 14(2) and Recital 34, which cover AI companions and chatbots deployed as a functionality
      of online games and platforms, including where in-game purchases can occur.
    improvement: Default the assistant to off (or teacher-enabled), place it behind a neutral help entry, and add a visible "turn off assistant" setting.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '(assistantEnabled|chatbotEnabled|aiChatEnabled|aiCompanionEnabled|autoOpenChat|autoStartAssistant|showAssistantOnStart)\s*[:=]\s*true'}

  - id: CORE-AI-11
    title: AI never nudges children to spend or towards ads
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      AI tutors, characters and assistants never suggest purchases, upgrades, premium content or
      advertised products, and are not optimised for spending or engagement time.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Recital 31 names AI-enhanced nudging as a commercial tactic with particular effects on minors;
      Art. 14(1)(c) applies the economic transaction safeguards to AI companions and chatbots, and Recital 34
      extends safeguards to chatbots inside games with in-game purchases. AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) bans AI that
      exploits age-related vulnerability.
    improvement: Remove commercial goals from system prompts and fine-tuning data; add red-team prompts that try to elicit upsell and test that the AI refuses.
    effort: low
    sources: [KIDS, AIA, UCPD]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(upsell|encourage (the )?(user|child|student|player) to (buy|purchase|upgrade|subscribe)|promote (the )?(premium|shop|store|subscription))'}

  - id: CORE-AI-12
    title: Generative features cannot depict real people
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      Generative features cannot make images, video or voices of real, identifiable people, other children
      above all. In practice: (1) no photo, video or voice recording of a person goes into generation, and
      there is no face swap, voice cloning or editing of photos of people; (2) prompts that name someone on the
      class list, or another real person, are refused, checked against the roster inside the product; (3)
      uploaded images are checked for faces and refused for generation, without identifying anyone; (4)
      generated media is labelled as made by AI and carries provenance data; and (5) a child can report "this
      is about me", and that report is handled first.
    rationale: >
      A classmate's face or voice is personal data, and nobody in the class can consent for them (GDPR Art. 5
      and 6; CORE-DAT-14). The EU action plan against cyberbullying names deepfake abuse. Directive (EU)
      2024/1385 requires Member States to make sexual deepfakes a crime, and the AI Omnibus adds a ban on AI
      systems that generate non-consensual intimate images. Labels follow AI Act Art. 50. Blocking real
      people at the input is far more reliable than filtering the output.
    improvement: Remove image-to-image, face swap and voice cloning from child-facing features; check prompts against the class roster; refuse uploads with faces for generation; add provenance metadata (for example C2PA) and a priority "this is about me" report.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, AIA, AIA-OMNIBUS, VAW-DIR, CB-AP]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: dependency, confidence: medium, names: [insightface, facefusion, roop, simswap, deepfacelab, faceswap, rvc-python, so-vits-svc-fork, openvoice]}
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(face_?swap|swap_?face|voice_?clon|clone_?voice|img2img|image_?to_?image)'}


  # ================================================================ COMMUNICATIONS (KIDS Act Art. 12, 15(2), Recital 36; DSA)
  # Detection uses the communications inventory (tooling/comms.py). Absence of a safeguard in code is a
  # signal, not proof: many chat services configure moderation in a dashboard. Findings are REVIEW.
  - id: CORE-CHT-01
    title: Every communication channel is declared
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Every way children can communicate or act towards each other is declared in csef.yaml features and
      listed in the DPIA, with the service used and where data is processed. That includes text chat, direct
      messages, comments, voice, video and live streaming, and also channels without text: emotes and
      reactions, avatar names and looks, drawings and shared creations, and actions in shared worlds
      (building, destroying, following or trapping another child's avatar).
    rationale: >
      Accountability (GDPR Art. 5(2)) and the DPIA require knowing every channel. Contact risks are the main
      reason the KIDS Act regulates online games (Recital 36). Bullying uses whatever channel exists, words or
      not. Undeclared channels escape every other check.
    improvement: Add the channel to `features` (chat, multiplayer, social or ugc) and to `third_parties`; list non-text channels too; update the DPIA.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, KIDS, DSA-G28]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_undeclared, confidence: high}


  - id: CORE-CHT-02
    title: Report and block in every channel
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      In every channel, those without text included (CORE-CHT-01), a child can report a message, a creation
      or a user in one step, and block any user without the blocked user being told who blocked them. The
      reported content is kept as evidence for the person who handles it. What the child hears after a
      report is in CORE-SAF-06.
    rationale: >
      DSA Art. 16 (notice and action) applies to hosting services. KIDS Act Art. 12(1)(d) (block without
      identity disclosed) and Art. 19 (child-friendly reporting). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.
    improvement: Add report and block actions to every message, creation and profile; route reports to a moderation queue with priority for minors.
    effort: medium
    sources: [DSA, KIDS, DSA-G28]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_report_block, confidence: medium}


  - id: CORE-CHT-03
    title: Moderation by people and by tools
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Communication is moderated by named people (a teacher in school use, trained moderators otherwise) who can
      hide, remove, mute and suspend, supported by automated filters for text and images in the product's
      languages, with rate limits against spam. The level of moderation matches the age band.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Recital 36 lists cyberbullying, harassment, grooming, sexual exploitation, recruitment and
      radicalisation as contact risks in online games. DSA Art. 28 guidelines on moderation for minors.
    improvement: Give teachers or moderators hide/remove/mute/suspend powers; add a text filter (word list plus a moderation API) and image checks for uploads; add rate limits.
    effort: high
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28, DSA]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_moderation, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-CHT-04
    title: Direct messages only with approved contacts; groups only with agreement
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Nobody can start a private conversation with a child unless the child (or, under 13, the guardian or
      teacher) has approved that contact. Children are added to groups only with their agreement. Nobody can
      pressure a child into approving contact.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 12(1)(a)(c) and 12(2), applied to online games by Art. 15(1)(c) for 12(1).
    improvement: Restrict direct messages to approved contacts within the class or group; require acceptance for group invitations.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_direct_messages, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-CHT-05
    title: No links, handles or contact details in children's messages
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Messages to and from children block or warn on external links, social media handles, phone numbers,
      emails and addresses, so the product cannot be used to move children to other services.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Art. 15(2) and Recital 36 (restrict link-outs, warning messages, prevent enticing minors to other
      services); Art. 12(3)(c) (contact details of minors never shared).
    improvement: Filter URLs, handles and contact details before delivery; show a warning to the child and notify moderation.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_link_filter, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-CHT-06
    title: Voice, video and live streaming off by default
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    requirement: >
      Voice chat, video chat and live streaming are off by default, enabled only by a guardian or teacher for
      under-13s, limited to approved contacts, and children cannot host live streams by default.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 11(1) (camera, microphone) and Art. 12(3)(f) (no hosting of real-time transmissions by default). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.
    improvement: Default voice and video to off; add guardian or teacher activation; restrict to class groups; remove child-hosted streaming.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_voice_default_on, confidence: high}
        - {type: repo, check: comms_voice_video, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-CHT-07
    title: Children's shared media is protected
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Images and files sent in messages are checked automatically, visible to the responsible teacher or
      moderator, and cannot be downloaded or forwarded by other users. Contact and account information of
      children is never visible to people they have not accepted.
    rationale: KIDS Act Art. 12(3)(a)(b)(e). DSA Art. 28 guidelines.
    improvement: Add image checks on upload, disable download and forwarding of children's media, and restrict profile visibility.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28, GDPR]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: repo, check: comms_media, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-CHT-08
    title: Safeguarding procedure with a route for each kind of harm
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication, survey, ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      There is a written safeguarding procedure with a named lead. It sets a route for each kind of harm:
      grooming, sexual exploitation, extortion, threats, self-harm signals and radicalisation in
      communication; and disclosures of harm (abuse, self-harm, bullying, danger at home) in free-text or voice
      answers, drawings and AI conversations. It says how each is recognised and escalated, how evidence is
      kept, and when guardians, schools, hotlines and authorities are contacted. A disclosure goes to the
      safeguarding lead named by the school, never automatically to guardians (who may be the source of
      harm) or to peers, and the child sees in age-appropriate words where to get help now. No AI analysis
      scans answers for risk without a DPIA and human review. Moderators are trained and supported. Bullying
      between children follows CORE-CHT-15.
    rationale: >
      KIDS Act Recital 36 names these contact risks. Children disclose in unexpected places, and a disclosure
      left in a log or sent to the wrong adult can put the child in danger (UN General Comment 25). National
      child-protection law decides who must act. Code cannot show this; it is the human side of every other
      communication rule. Merges CORE-SAF-11 (retired in 0.11.0).
    improvement: Write the procedure with the DPO and a safeguarding lead; agree a disclosure route with each school; prefer closed answers where free text is not needed; train moderators and teachers; test the procedure with a tabletop exercise each year.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28, UNCRC-GC25, BIK]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: survey_free_text_without_route, confidence: high}


  - id: CORE-CHT-09
    title: Messages are kept only as long as needed
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Messages have a defined retention period enforced by code, children and teachers can delete them, and
      reported messages are preserved only for the investigation.
    rationale: GDPR storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) and erasure (Art. 17).
    improvement: Add a retention job for messages and keep reported messages in a separate, access-controlled store.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    detection:
      method: manual
  - id: CORE-CHT-10
    title: Reports stay confidential
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Do not show who reported. The reported child, other children and their guardians are never told who
      made a report, and nothing in the product lets them work it out: no "reported by" label, no shared
      report count, no action timed to point at one child. Only the person handling the report, and the
      safeguarding lead where needed, can see the reporter. If the school's procedure later needs the
      reporter's name, the reporter and their guardian are told first.
    rationale: >
      Fear of being found out stops children from reporting. The EDPB says notice mechanisms should allow,
      but not require, identifying the notifier, and reveal the identity to the affected user only where
      strictly necessary. The KIDS Act proposal already protects the identity of whoever blocks (Art.
      12(1)(d)), but no law says the same for every product's reports, so this is a SHOULD.
    improvement: Remove reporter names from every view the reported child or peers can see; batch or delay visible moderation actions; limit reporter identity to the moderator role.
    effort: low
    sources: [EDPB-DSAGDPR, GDPR, CB-AP, KIDS]
    detection:
      method: manual


  - id: CORE-CHT-11
    title: Children can report for a friend; misuse is handled by people
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      A child can report something that happens to someone else ("this is happening to a friend"), from the
      same place as any report, without the friend's permission and without proof. The friend is offered
      help privately, and the report follows CORE-SAF-06 and CORE-CHT-10. Good practice: (1) the flow asks
      what happened, nothing more; (2) a report made in good faith that turns out unfounded never counts
      against the child; (3) only repeated reports that a person finds manifestly unfounded are recorded,
      seen only by the moderator or teacher and never by other children; (4) the child first gets a kind
      warning that explains why, before any limit; (5) there are no automatic sanctions; and (6) many reports
      against the same child by a group are treated as a possible sign of bullying, not as proof against
      that child.
    rationale: >
      Bystanders often see what adults do not, and the EU action plan against cyberbullying asks that
      reporting and support reach bystanders. DSA Art. 23 lets online platforms, after a warning, stop
      handling notices from people who often send manifestly unfounded ones; for children the answer is a
      conversation with an adult, not a penalty. Reporting itself can be used to bully, so patterns matter
      more than counts.
    improvement: Add "this is happening to someone else" to the report flow and a private help message for the friend; record manifestly unfounded reports for the moderator only, with a warning step and no automatic sanctions; flag group reports against one child for review.
    effort: medium
    sources: [CB-AP, DSA, UNCRC-GC25]
    detection:
      method: manual


  - id: CORE-CHT-12
    title: No design that lets children exclude, rank or expose each other
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      The design gives children no tools to exclude, rank or expose each other: (1) no voting a child out of
      a game, team or group, and no removal of players by other players; only the teacher or a moderator
      can remove; (2) no ratings of children by children (stars, scores or likes on a person, "best" or
      "worst" player votes); feedback on someone's work uses preset kind options or a rubric the teacher can
      see; (3) no polls or questions about classmates; (4) teams and pairs are made by the teacher or by the
      product (at random or balanced), never picked by children in front of others, and nobody sees the order
      of choice; (5) paid or premium items do not show status to classmates, and the school can turn their
      display off; (6) friend lists, friend counts and online status are not shown to other children; and (7)
      the teacher can keep two children apart in pairings and groups without anyone seeing why.
    rationale: >
      The EU common definition of cyberbullying includes social exclusion. Most cyberbullying comes from
      peers the child knows from school, so closed class groups keep strangers out but not the bully.
      Design that lets children vote others out, rate each other or show status hands them that power. Not
      law as such, so a SHOULD. Related: CORE-SAF-10 (no follower counts or likes on appearance), C-ENG-02
      (leaderboards).
    improvement: Replace vote-kick with removal by the teacher or a moderator; remove ratings of people and polls about classmates; make teams by teacher choice or at random; hide paid status and friend counts in school use; add a "keep apart" setting for teachers.
    effort: medium
    sources: [CB-AP, UNCRC-GC25, R-JUVONEN2008, R-WOLKE2017]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(vote_?kick|kick_?vote|vote_?to_?kick|rate_?(player|classmate|student)|player_?rating|popularity_?(poll|vote|rank)|hot_?or_?not)'}


  - id: CORE-CHT-13
    title: Children can keep evidence and reach national help
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      A child who reports can keep a record of what happened inside the product (what was said or done,
      when, by which account), see it later and share it with a trusted adult, the school or a helpline,
      without downloading or forwarding other children's media (CORE-CHT-07). The product links to the
      national child helpline (116 111) and Safer Internet Centre, and connects its reporting and support to
      the EU online safety app through the app's interface where the country offers it. The record follows
      the retention rules (CORE-CHT-09).
    rationale: >
      The EU action plan against cyberbullying plans an app where children report to a national helpline,
      store and pass on evidence and get help, and which platforms can connect to their reporting and support
      tools through APIs. The KIDS Act proposal asks Member States for free, confidential national channels
      that complement providers' reporting tools. Not yet an obligation for providers, so a SHOULD.
    improvement: Add a "my reports" view with the evidence record and a share option to a trusted adult or helpline; add national helpline links; plan the connection to the national app.
    effort: medium
    sources: [CB-AP, KIDS, BIK]
    detection:
      method: manual


  - id: CORE-CHT-14
    title: Communication is open only when someone can respond
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      The product says who handles reports (the teacher, the provider's moderators or both), in which hours
      and languages, and how fast: for example urgent safety reports within one hour and other reports
      within one school day while communication is open. Outside those hours communication is closed,
      limited to preset messages, or covered by the provider's moderators. Teachers can set open hours for
      their class. A child who reports is told when to expect an answer. The cover is declared in csef.yaml
      (`moderation`) and checked against real response times.
    rationale: >
      A report nobody reads protects nobody. When the teacher is the moderator, chat that stays open in the
      evening has no one behind it. KIDS Act Art. 19 and the DSA Art. 28 guidelines expect reports to be
      handled promptly. CORE-CHT-03 names the people; this rule makes sure their time covers the hours the
      channel is open. What the product can safely offer depends on who can respond.
    improvement: Add open hours set by the teacher; close or limit communication outside covered hours; declare `moderation` in csef.yaml and measure response times.
    effort: medium
    sources: [KIDS, DSA-G28, CB-AP]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: moderation_coverage_missing, confidence: medium}


  - id: CORE-CHT-15
    title: Bullying between children follows the school's procedure, or a default one
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    age_bands: [all]
    features: [communication]
    requirement: >
      Strongly recommended. A report about bullying between children goes to the person named in the
      school's anti-bullying plan or procedure, not to the authorities and not straight to guardians. If the
      school has no plan, the product offers a default procedure that the school accepts at set-up
      (templates/bullying-procedure.md): who is told, how to listen to both children, how to keep them apart
      in the product (CORE-CHT-12), how guardians are informed through the school, when to check again, and
      when it becomes a safeguarding matter (CORE-CHT-08). Report categories follow the EU common definition
      of cyberbullying (humiliating, excluding, abusing, harassing or harming, once or repeated) in words for
      children, and the school sees totals per category for its classes, never figures that point to one
      child (at least 5 per figure, as in CORE-DAT-17).
    rationale: >
      Most online bullying is between children who know each other from school, so the school is usually the
      right place to act. Many schools have an anti-bullying plan (in Portugal, "Escola Sem Bullying. Escola
      Sem Violência"), but not all, so the product must work without one. Shared categories let schools and
      Member States compare data, as the EU action plan asks. Not law, so a SHOULD, but strongly recommended
      for any product with communication.
    improvement: Ask at set-up for the school's anti-bullying contact, or for acceptance of the default procedure; route bullying reports there; use the EU-definition categories; give schools totals by class and school.
    effort: medium
    sources: [CB-AP, UNCRC-GC25, R-JUVONEN2008]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: bullying_route_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CPC-VC
    title: "CPC Network: Key Principles on In-game Virtual Currencies (21 March 2025)"
    type: guidance
    jurisdiction: EU
    status: "Published 21 Mar 2025 by the EU consumer protection authorities (CPC Network), coordinated by the Commission. # Topic map for comparing codes of conduct with CSEF (used by tooling/coc.py).
#
# For each rule:
#   terms     groups of synonyms. A clause "covers" the rule when it matches at least two groups
#             (or the only group) with committing language (must, shall, will, never, do not...).
#   conflict  subject terms. A sentence that mentions one of them with permissive language
#             (may, can, allowed, permitted, optional, provided that...) and no negation is flagged
#             as a possible conflict for a person to review.
#   conflict_regex  extra patterns that signal a conflict on their own (e.g. "enabled by default").
#   skip      engineering-internal rules a code of conduct is not expected to cover.
# Matching is case-insensitive, ignores accents and hyphens, and is in English. For codes in other
# languages, translate first or use the csef-review skill, which compares meaning, not words.

# CSEF Literacy Compass: target catalogue. Single source of truth for tooling/compass.py.
#
# The Compass asks a different question from the CSEF rules. The rules ask "does the product do harm?".
# The Compass asks "what does the product teach about digital life, and how do we know?".
#
# Two lenses:
#   learner  what learners should know and be able to do (DigComp 3.0, AILit, UNESCO MIL and AI frameworks).
#            Evaluated when the product claims the axis or target (csef.yaml `compass.claims`, or a claim found
#            in the documents). Otherwise shown as an opportunity, never as a failure.
#   design   what the product itself teaches by how it is built and supported ("literacy by design").
#            Universal targets apply to every product used by children; feature targets apply when the
#            product has the feature (same feature names as csef.yaml).
#
# Evidence ladder, per target (never a total score, never a ranking):
#   0 Not found   1 Stated   2 Designed   3 Tested   4 Measured
#
# Field reference:
#   id            AXIS-NN
#   scope         claimed | universal | feature
#   features      for scope feature: applies if any is declared. For claimed targets: features that make the
#                 target a natural opportunity (suggest_when).
#   refs          competence framework references (shown in reports, used for crosswalks)
#   sources       ids from framework/sources.yaml or a loaded pack
#   terms         groups of synonyms (English and European Portuguese). A passage matches when it matches
#                 `need` groups (default: all groups, at most 2).
#   conflict      phrases that teach the opposite of the target (hidden curriculum). Found = possible conflict.
#   ideas         short design patterns, mostly for games
#
# Matching ignores case, accents and hyphens. The csef-review skill reviews meaning in any language.
# Licence: CC BY 4.0

version: "0.1.0"

axes:
  - id: INF
    title: Information and media
    lens: learner
    question: Does it help learners find, judge and use information and media, including AI-generated content?
    sources: [DIGCOMP3, UNESCO-MIL, UNESCO-AIMIL]
  - id: COM
    title: Communication, citizenship and rights
    lens: learner
    question: Does it help learners interact well, take part as citizens and know their rights?
    sources: [DIGCOMP3, UNESCO-MIL, UNCRC-GC25]
  - id: CRE
    title: Creation and computational thinking
    lens: learner
    question: Does it help learners create, remix responsibly and think computationally?
    sources: [DIGCOMP3]
  - id: SAF
    title: Safety, privacy and wellbeing
    lens: learner
    question: Does it help learners stay safe, protect their data, manage money and balance their use?
    sources: [DIGCOMP3, BIK, IEEE3527]
  - id: PRB
    title: Problem solving and learning to learn
    lens: learner
    question: Does it help learners solve problems, choose tools and reflect on their own digital skills?
    sources: [DIGCOMP3, AILIT]
  - id: AI
    title: AI literacy
    lens: learner
    question: Does it help learners engage with, create with, manage and shape AI?
    sources: [AILIT, UNESCO-AICFS, DIGCOMP3]
  - id: TRN
    title: Transparency that teaches
    lens: design
    question: Does the product explain itself to children in a way that builds literacy, and avoid teaching the opposite?
    sources: [GDPR, AIA, DSA-G28, KIDS, UNCRC-GC25]
  - id: EDU
    title: Educator and family enablement
    lens: design
    question: Can teachers and families turn use into learning, and see that learning happened?
    sources: [EU-DEC, ET4G2, AILIT]

evidence_levels:
  0: {name: Not found, meaning: "Nothing in the documents addresses the target."}
  1: {name: Stated, meaning: "The documents name the target or claim it, without saying how the product achieves it."}
  2: {name: Designed, meaning: "Specific activities, mechanics, features or teacher materials are linked to the target."}
  3: {name: Tested, meaning: "The design was tried with learners or teachers (pilot, playtest, co-design) and results are recorded."}
  4: {name: Measured, meaning: "Learning outcomes were measured (pre/post, comparison group, independent evaluation)."}

  topics:
